samples.text:
The pie charts give information about why male and female workers left their job in a big company in 2024.

Firstly, for men the most common reason was better salary in another place, with 38%. Career progression was the second reason at 24%. Work-life balance was 12% and relocation and retirement was both 10%. Only 6% of men leaved because of family reasons. So for men, salary and career was clearly more important than the other reasons.

For women, the picture is different. The biggest reason was work-life balance with 23%, and better salary was nearly the same at 22%. Also family reasons was very important for women, it was 21%, which is much more higher than for men. Career progression was 19%, relocation 9% and retirement only 6%.

Overall, men mostly left their jobs because of money and career, but women had more different reasons and the family and work-life balance were more important to them than to men. Relocation was similar for both genders.
samples.why: Accurate coverage of both charts · overview placed at the end and fairly general · mechanical sequencing (Firstly, Also) · some repetition · several verb form, agreement and comparative errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The two pie charts compare the main reasons given by men and women for leaving their jobs at a large company in 2024.

Overall, male employees were mainly motivated by financial and career considerations, whereas female employees' reasons were spread more evenly, with work-life balance and family matters playing a much larger role.

Among men, the single most common reason was a better salary elsewhere, cited by 38%, followed by career progression at 24%. Together, these two factors accounted for almost two-thirds of male departures. Work-life balance was mentioned by 12% of men, while relocation and retirement each represented 10%. Family reasons were the least significant, at only 6%.

For women, by contrast, no single reason dominated. Work-life balance was the top reason (23%), closely followed by a better salary (22%) and family reasons (21%), the latter being more than three times the figure for men. Career progression was slightly less important, at 19%. Relocation had a similar share for both sexes (9% for women), and retirement was the least frequent reason for female employees, at 6%.
samples.why: Clear overview contrasting the two groups · key differences highlighted and supported with figures · logical organisation by gender · good range of linking and comparison language · few errors.

samples.text:
The charts break down the reasons why male and female staff resigned from a large company in 2024.

The most striking contrast is that men left overwhelmingly for pay and promotion, while women's departures were distributed far more evenly across several motives, among which work-life balance and family commitments featured prominently.

For male employees, a better salary elsewhere was by far the leading factor, at 38%, and career progression accounted for a further 24%, meaning that these two reasons together explained 62% of resignations. Work-life balance lagged well behind at 12%, and relocation and retirement were each responsible for 10%, while family reasons were the least cited, at just 6%.

Among female employees, the pattern was much flatter. Work-life balance ranked first with 23%, but it was only marginally ahead of better pay (22%) and family reasons (21%), and career progression was not far behind at 19%. The gender gap was widest for family reasons, which were more than three times as common among women as among men, and for salary, where the male figure was 16 points higher. By contrast, relocation was almost identical for the two groups, at 10% and 9%, and retirement was less common among women (6%).
samples.why: Skilful selection of the key contrasts · clear overview · figures used selectively for comparison (gap of 16 points, three times) · smooth cohesion · precise, natural vocabulary · wide range of accurate structures.
